title: The lion inside
hook: Rumi ends: the outer enemy is gone, the lion within remains, the greater struggle (Masnavi 1.1373ff)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lion leaped at his own reflection and drowned. Your line was that's my face. Did you look into the well before you leaped? Day one hundred eighty-one.

You finally deal with the thing. You quit the job with the awful boss. You move out of the apartment with the terrible roommate. You block the person who kept upsetting you. And for a week, it's wonderful. Then, slowly, you notice that the anger is still there. The worry is still there. The old habit is right where you left it. The problem, it turns out, packed its bags and came along. The animals are dancing in the valley. The lion is gone. And Rumi, instead of ending the story, turns and speaks straight to his listeners. Today, the lion inside.
screen: `YOU FINALLY DEAL WITH THE THING.` → `IT PACKED ITS BAGS AND CAME ALONG.` → `THE LION INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Rumi's turn goes like this, in plain words. We've killed the enemy outside. But inside there's an enemy worse than him. And the clever hare can't trick this one into a well. Wit and reason alone won't defeat it. What is this inner lion? Rumi's word is nafs. In Arabic and Persian it means the self or the soul, and in Sufi teaching it often means the grasping, demanding part of the self: the appetite that is never full, the pride that has to win, the anger that roars first. Rumi calls it a dragon that only sleeps when it's weak, and wakes when it gets the chance. Then he tells a story about the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, coming home from a battle and saying: we have returned from the lesser struggle to the greater struggle. The word there is jihad, which means striving or struggle. The greater one, in this saying, is the struggle with your own self. Honesty note: this saying is famous and much loved among Sufis, but many hadith scholars say its chain of transmission is weak, and it isn't in the major collections. Rumi uses it, and many Muslims treasure its meaning; others question its source. Both are true. Now put the whole story together. A lion, a clever hare, a well, a reflection. The outer lion was never really the danger. The one to watch is the one you carry everywhere, the one who would have leaped at the reflection too. That's the greater struggle, for every person on every path. The lion inside.
screen: `AN ENEMY WORSE, WITHIN.` · `NAFS: THE GRASPING SELF.` · `THE LESSER AND GREATER STRUGGLE.` · `A LOVED SAYING, A WEAK CHAIN.` · then, large: `THE LION INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your inner lion. Settle, and breathe. Ask quietly: what in me roars first? Maybe it's anger. Maybe it's wanting more, or needing to be right, or fear dressed up as control. Don't fight it now. Just see it and give it a name, the way you'd name an animal you're going to learn to live with. Then breathe into your belly, slow and low, and feel how much stronger you are when you're still. The bell holds the time.
The lion inside. Rumi's turn at the end of the story: the outer enemy is gone, but the grasping self remains, and struggling with it is the greater struggle. Today's word.
Your line: the lion inside. Today, when your inner lion starts to roar, call it by its name, take one slow breath, and choose your next move. Day one hundred eighty-one.

howItsDone: In Sufi teaching, the struggle with the nafs, the grasping self, is described as the greater jihad, and the end of Rumi's lion and hare story is often read as the classic statement of it.

original.note: Arabic and Persian: self, soul; in Sufi teaching, often the grasping, lower self.
